checks: Verified provenance in 6c56e9569b9982d7 opening, (1)–(2), §3, (7)–(11), and §6, (13), and 4202609a15fa8f99 §1, (2)–(4) and its concluding discussion. Both raw source digests match.

Rechecked the exact revised bytes and confirmed that the statement and all cap equality, cover and converse arguments are unchanged. The revised opening directly derives both local premises and removes the two duplicate same-batch dependencies.

For an interior mark y, the through-cut is proper and has positive section measure, including counting measure one in dimension one. In accepted §2 set the base variation to zero, continuous normal variation to w and threshold variation to w·y. Each perturbed normal remains nonzero near zero and its cut passes through y, so it cannot have lower volume than the active cap. The resulting two-sided derivative is positive coarea times w·(section centroid−y). Vanishing for all w gives the centroid identity. Section 2 is a local finite sum of single-fiber variations and does not use the ambient depth-region interior or the projected contact assumptions.

The revised existence and uniqueness step is valid: joint cap continuity and compactness give an attained maximum, and an interior inball versus a boundary supporting halfspace puts every deepest mark in the interior. At the midpoint of two deepest marks, an attaining cap has mass at most their common depth. If thresholds differ, a positive-volume slab makes its stricter endpoint cap smaller, contradicting that endpoint depth. If thresholds agree, the cap is active at both because it has mass at least their common depth, and its one section cannot have both centroids. In dimension one distinct marks always give different thresholds.

Endpoint maximizers exist uniquely and are interior. Their inballs combine to make the weighted mark interior to the sum and N. The real-base hull is full-dimensional: an open subset is formed over the open base interval by the continuous interpolation of the endpoint inballs. Its fiber is the exact Minkowski interpolation by convexity of K and L. Apply root concavity, dilate by s+t and use monotonicity into N; equality makes the weighted mark the unique deepest point of N.

At an arbitrary active N direction through the weighted mark, addition of cap margins gives inclusion of the Minkowski sum of endpoint caps in the N cap. Equality of the first and last terms in the volume-root chain forces equality throughout; positivity of s,t forces each endpoint cap separately to attain its own maximum depth. Full-dimensionality follows from positive cap volumes. Equal volume of the included compact convex bodies makes them equal as sets.

Brunn–Minkowski equality makes the endpoint caps positively homothetic, with scale r fixed by the ratio of their own maximal depths. Gardner, The Brunn–Minkowski Inequality, Theorem 4.1 and the compact convex equality discussion in §4, supplies the equality case: https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~carlier/Brunn-Minkowski. In d=1 positive caps are intervals and the equality condition holds directly.

The minimizing exposed face of each endpoint cap is its nonempty through-mark section. Positive homothety takes that face to the other and takes its centroid to the other centroid. The section centroids are the marks, so the translation is exactly g_L−r g_K, independent of direction; in d=1 these sections are singleton faces.

Use finitely many active normals balanced at g. Positive balance gives a covering family of ordinary halfspaces at any common translation, so the endpoint traces cover K and L with the same affine map and their union gives the claimed whole-body homothety. The target traces cover N and each is the exact weighted sum of endpoint traces, hence lies inside sK+tL. The opposite inclusion is a hypothesis. The per-active-direction assertion was proved before restricting to the finite cover.

The converse follows from translation invariance and d-homogeneity, and the ordinary volume-root equality conditions are identical by classical Brunn–Minkowski and strict volume monotonicity. For parallel affine planes the weighted sum of origins lies in the plane of N because the sum affinely spans a parallel d-plane contained in that plane; translation to their common vector space preserves inclusion, caps and intrinsic volumes.

dependencies.mapping: Use n=1 and C=conv(({0}×K)∪({1}×L)), a convex body with nonempty ambient interior from interpolating the endpoint inballs. Assertions 1 and 2 apply to the endpoint marks and their interpolation at lambda=t/(s+t). Its fiber is (1−lambda)K+lambda L; dilating by s+t converts the raw depth root homogeneously to the weighted Minkowski sum, and containment in N transfers the inequality.

Set n=1, P={0} and K_0 equal to the body in question. The family is compatible because conv({0}×B)={0}×B and total mass is positive. For a nonzero continuous normal the base term vanishes identically, so c_0(u,u·g) is exactly the ordinary cap volume; pure-base containing cuts capture the whole body and cannot lower the minimum. The actual deepest mark therefore meets the hypotheses. The finite active collection has positive coefficients summing its normals to zero, and its ordinary closed traces cover the plane, including in d=1. Use B=N at its weighted maximizing mark. The positive balance then gives the same-direction ordinary covers at the endpoint marks.

Invoke the one-fiber component of §2 at a proper through-mark section of each relevant ordinary convex body. Take the continuous normal and threshold perturbations to be (w,w·y) at the mark y and no base perturbation. There are no nonproper fibers, the normal has initial unit length, and the section measure is positive. This is the local first-variation formula, not the projected contact theorem, so ambient interior of a mixed depth region is unnecessary. Stationarity gives the ordinary centroid conclusion; the revised proof then establishes uniqueness independently.
